content_voiceover: This slide lists the factors that predict a poor prognosis in osteosarcoma, and these show up frequently on boards as the features that should raise your concern for a worse outcome. The single most important one is detectable metastatic disease at diagnosis, and the lung is by far the most common site of metastasis in osteosarcoma, so a baseline chest CT is essential at diagnosis. Larger primary tumor size is also unfavorable, bigger tumors carry more risk. Axial skeletal primaries, meaning tumors of the spine, pelvis, or skull rather than the extremities, tend to do worse, partly because they're harder to resect completely. Similarly, a proximal location within the limb, closer to the trunk, carries worse prognosis than a distal one, again largely because achieving a wide surgical margin is more difficult. Incomplete resection, meaning positive or close margins after surgery, is a major adverse factor since local control is critical in a radioresistant tumor. And finally, a poor histologic response to preoperative chemotherapy, meaning a high percentage of viable tumor remaining at the time of surgery, predicts a higher risk of relapse and worse survival.
keypoints: Detectable metastatic disease at diagnosis, most commonly to lung, is the strongest adverse factor
Axial skeletal or proximal limb primaries are harder to resect and carry worse outcomes
Incomplete surgical resection is a major adverse prognostic factor
Poor histologic response to preoperative chemotherapy predicts higher relapse risk
keypoint_voiceover: For osteosarcoma prognosis, remember metastatic disease at diagnosis, especially to lung, larger tumor size, axial or proximal primaries, incomplete resection, and poor histologic response to preoperative chemo as the key adverse factors.
